"So colony losses are trending up. This loss is only sustainable through active and aggressive colony splitting by beekeepers to attempt to stay ahead of dead colonies."

The 2024-2025 die-off, the Honey Bee Health Coalition reported, represents an

, including reduced honey production, lost pollination income, and the cost of replacing dead colonies. This crisis is the result of a structural problem in bee farming that's been building for decades.

As David Burrows, founder of Arkearth Inc., a Dallas-based pollinator nonprofit, explains, commercial beekeeping in the U.S. runs on a system that has never been particularly gentle on bees. Each winter and early spring, beekeepers load their hives onto 18-wheelers and haul them, sometimes from as far as Florida or Michigan, to California, where they pollinate the state's almond crop within a window of ten days or fewer.
California produces 80% of the world's almond supply, and without bees, that crop simply wouldn't exist
. But the constant cross-country transit spreads disease. "Imagine being at a busy airport," Burrows says. "That's basically what's happening with the bees."

The monoculture conditions of feasting on just one plant are just as damaging, a diet he compares to a person eating nothing but Chex Mix for two weeks. "It's like having a healthy buffet versus just eating one thing for two weeks," Burrows says. "They're not getting a broad spectrum of nutrients, which weakens their immune systems."

So while they may survive, they're not thriving, and a weakened immune system is no match for varroa mites already resistant to treatment. "They're alive, but just by a thread," Wilson-Rich adds, meaning "they're not producing." The USDA, he explains, calls this a sublethal effect, a colony that registers as present in the count but is far too depleted to contribute meaningfully to honey output.
There's one more stressor to add to the list: climate change.

All of this is making it nearly impossible for some smaller honey operations to stay solvent. "These factors, coupled with the need to make a large number of replacement colonies to replace the dead ones, have created a situation where it is difficult for keepers to remain profitable," Gilbert says.
Why imported honey is creating a new problem

To fill the growing gap, the U.S. has leaned heavily on imports and has been a net importer of honey since the '90s. In 2023, imported honey accounted for 73% of the total domestic supply. The following year, the U.S. imported more than 562 million pounds from abroad, worth roughly $650 million, primarily from India, Argentina, and Brazil. While it's filling grocery shelves, this cheaper foreign honey has undercut domestic beekeepers, who can't compete with imported honey priced as low as 84 cents a pound, according to the USDA's National Honey Report, when domestic production averages $2.69 per pound.

While there may be imported honey on the shelves, not all of it is what you think it is. Our growing taste for honey has made it one of the most adulterated foods worldwide, with some producers substituting corn or rice syrup and selling the mixture as the real thing.

"If you see something on a store shelf that says it's pure honey and it's only $3.80, it probably should be closer to $12 or $15," Burrows says, calling it the biggest red flag to watch for in the honey aisle. It's a problem the bipartisan Honey Integrity Act, introduced in Congress in March 2025, is now trying to address, though it's been sitting with the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions for more than a year.

As for what you can do, the answer is simple: buy local, and pay what real honey actually costs. "Support your local beekeeper," Wilson-Rich says. "Local honey is the most flavorful. It connects to the terroir of your land."
The bees kept their end of the bargain for a long time. "If you eat food or breathe air, you need bees," Wilson-Rich says. Right now, they need us back.
